contentHtml:
India’s healthcare story is rightly celebrated on the global stage. Having earned our reputation as the ‘pharmacy of the world’, we are now charting a bold new chapter in health-technology, digital public infrastructure, and AI-driven diagnostics. Yet, after spending nearly two decades working across India’s public health and nutrition landscape, I keep returning to an underlying biological truth that no algorithm can bypass- you cannot engineer lifelong health in an emergency room, nor can you course-correct human development once pregnancy is already underway.

India is the most populous country, yet consider the numbers we are up against. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) now account for over 63% of all deaths in India, up from 38% in 1990, and are projected to cost the Indian economy $4.58 trillion by 2030. Simultaneously, we are facing a rapidly escalating double burden of malnutrition. According to the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5), 57% of Indian women of reproductive age and 59.1% of adolescent girls are anemic—while 24% of women aged 15–49 are now overweight or obese, nearly doubling from 12.6% fifteen years ago. Meanwhile, roughly one-third of our women still enter pregnancy underweight.

Advt

If India is to protect its demographic dividend and break this twin grip of undernutrition and metabolic disease, our health and nutrition architecture must make a decisive pivot upstream. True health and nutrition security does not start when a mother registers for antenatal care; it begins long before conception.Reactive vs Proactive planningFor generations, our maternal and child health programs have operated on a reactive clock, swinging into action only after a pregnancy is confirmed. Clinically speaking, that is already late. By the time an expectant mother walks into her first antenatal check-up, frequently in her second trimester, the most critical events of embryogenesis, neural tube closure, and early organ formation have already closed.

Recent studies in epigenetics reveal that the metabolic destiny of a child is heavily scripted by the nutritional and metabolic health of both parents well prior to conception. When a young woman enters pregnancy with depleted micronutrient stores, chronic inflammation, or excess adiposity, it triggers adverse fetal programming. A baby born under these conditions faces a dramatically higher lifetime risk of insulin resistance, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease, even before taking their first breath.

Tackling an Obesogenic EnvironmentThis biological vulnerability is being compounded by a rapid shift in how young Indians eat. Over the past decade, India’s ultra-processed food (UPF) sector has grown at a compound annual rate of over 13%, outpacing GDP growth and reshaping dietary habits across both urban and rural households. Packaged snacks, sugary beverages, and refined foods, high in salt, sugar, and unhealthy fats, devoid of essential micronutrients, are steadily displacing traditional, diverse diets.

Advt

When adolescents and young adults subsist on calorie-dense, nutrient-poor ultra-processed foods, we end up with a paradox: young prospective parents who are simultaneously overweight and micronutrient-deficient. Viewed through a preconception lens, curbing ultra-processed food consumption and restoring dietary quality among youth is not merely a lifestyle advisory; it is primary prevention against the next generation’s NCD epidemic.This is precisely where the newly launched SEHAT initiative (Science Excellence for Health through Agricultural Transformation)—a landmark convergence between the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) and the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR)—can become a game-changer. By directly linking agricultural innovation with public health outcomes, SEHAT validates indigenous, region-specific foods, promotes integrated farming systems, and scales biofortified, nutrient-dense crop varieties (such as iron- and zinc-rich millets, pulses, and cereals). Embedding biofortified staples and local functional foods into everyday household diets ensure that young women and men build micronutrient reserves naturally through their daily meals, long before pregnancy enters the picture.

Advt

Policy Alignment and Scientific StewardshipThe encouraging news is that India’s policy and research ecosystems are increasingly aligning around this lifecycle continuum. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare’s SUMAN Roadmap 2030 sets an uncompromising benchmark for zero preventable maternal and newborn deaths across 130 high-focus districts, backed by stronger referral networks and digital tracking via the JANANI portal.Hand in hand with this, the 2026 Anemia Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan Operational Guidelines mark a decisive shift from universal, blind prophylaxis toward a precision, screening-led 7x7x7 strategy. By upgrading to a T4 approach (Test, Treat, Talk, and Track), deploying digital invasive hemoglobinometers, and explicitly targeting women of reproductive age (20–49 years) alongside adolescents (10–19 years), our national guidelines finally acknowledge a core reality: we cannot conquer anemia in pregnancy if we do not build iron stores and nutritional resilience in young women years before they conceive.

Providing the scientific backbone to this shift is the ICMR–National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN). Through its food-based Dietary Guidelines for Indians, nutrient requirement benchmarks, and translational research on double-burden malnutrition, ICMR-NIN is generating the exact evidence needed to move from nutrient-centric pills to holistic, food-based lifecourse solutions. Equally critical is translating this science into clinical and community practice—by partnering with medical colleges, academic institutions, and state health systems to embed preconception nutrition into medical curricula, district-level implementation research, and community outreach. Professional medical bodies like the Federation of Obstetric and Gynaecological Societies of India (FOGSI) reinforce this clinical bridge through their Good Clinical Practice Recommendations on preconception care, emphasizing pre-pregnancy BMI optimization, metabolic screening, and timely micronutrient repletion.Lessons from the Ground: Scalable Models That WorkEncouragingly, we do not have to build this from scratch. Across India, targeted pilots and state-led initiatives offer clear proof of concept that can be scaled nationwide:

  • Maharashtra’s Nashik Preconception Care Model: Implemented in rural primary health centers in Nashik district, this initiative systematically tracked newlyweds and women planning a pregnancy through ASHA workers, providing BMI screening, hemoglobin testing, folic acid supplementation, and treatment for reproductive tract infections prior to conception. The model demonstrated measurable reductions in low-birth-weight deliveries and maternal anemia, proving that grassroots health workers can successfully deliver preconception care when given clear protocols.
  • Decentralized Community Nutrition Models (Odisha, Bihar, and Chhattisgarh): Under initiatives like Swabhimaan and state rural livelihood missions, women’s self-help groups (SHGs) have been mobilized to identify newlyweds and nutritionally vulnerable young women early linking them to nutri-gardens, poultry/dairy diversification, and targeted nutrition counseling before pregnancy occurs.
  • School-to-Community Adolescent Platforms: States like Tamil Nadu and Gujarat have shown how consistent Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation (WIFAS), paired with deworming and nutrition literacy in schools and anganwadis, builds a healthier metabolic baseline as adolescents transition into adulthood.

Bridging the Last-Mile GapWhile clinical protocols exist and isolated pilots have succeeded, preconception care still rarely reaches the average young couple visiting a public primary health center. To make it the bedrock of India’s health transformation, we must scale these lessons through three concrete shifts:

  • Turn Ayushman Arogya Mandirs into Preconception Wellness Hubs: Primary health centers, supported by regional medical colleges for mentoring and clinical audits, should offer structured pre-marital and preconception screening packages, checking hemoglobin, BMI, blood glucose, and blood pressure, so young adults enter parenthood metabolically resilient.
  • Connect Our Digital Health Stack Across the Lifecourse: Linking adolescent school health records with U-WIN, the Anemia Mukt Bharat portal, and maternal registries can ensure seamless continuity of care rather than fragmented, episodic interventions.
  • Reclaim Local Food Systems Through SEHAT and Community Platforms: Aligning the Eat Right movement and SEHAT’s biofortified agricultural push with Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Days (VHSNDs), public procurement systems, and women’s SHGs can shift households away from ultra-processed snacks toward nutrient-dense local staples.

India’s journey proves that when we combine scientific conviction with administrative scale, we change global paradigms. Applying that same ambition to preconception care and nutrition is our next great milestone. By uniting the research leadership of ICMR-NIN and medical colleges, the clinical precision of FOGSI, the agriculture-health convergence of SEHAT, and the systemic reach of SUMAN 2030 and Anemia Mukt Bharat 2026, we can halt the intergenerational transmission of both malnutrition and chronic disease at its source. True health security doesn’t begin in the delivery room. It begins the day we invest in the nutrition and metabolic health of our youth long before they ever become parents.This article is written by Shweta Khandelwal, Senior Public health nutrition expert, Centre for Chronic Disease Control (CCDC).(DISCLAIMER: The views expressed are solely of the author and ETHealthworld.com does not necessarily subscribe to it.
